The Snowflake provider lets
Terraform create, change and drop
Snowflake objects. Snowflake
maintains it under the source
address `snowflakedb/snowflake`
([provider docs](https://registry.
terraform.io/providers/snowflakedb
/snowflake/latest/docs)). The
provider works in SQL. It opens a
session, runs statements such as
`CREATE WAREHOUSE` or `GRANT`, and
reads objects back with `SHOW` and
`DESCRIBE`. The [Terraform
map](../terraform.md) explains
providers, state and plans in
general.

The unit is one Snowflake account,
seen through one session. Each
provider block opens one session,
as one user with one role. In
Snowflake, the role that creates
an object owns it ([object ownersh
ip](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/
user-guide/security-access-control
-overview)). So the provider role
owns everything that Terraform
creates ([One Session, One Role](#
one-session-one-role-one-session-o
ne-role)).

The provider has resources of two
kinds ([Objects and Edges](#object
s-and-edges-objects-and-edges)):

- An object resource stands for
one Snowflake object, such as a
database, a warehouse, a schema or
a storage integration. Its destroy
drops the object.
- An edge resource connects
objects that it does not own.
Grants, ownership transfers and
tag associations are edges. Their
destroy revokes or unsets.

Four more ideas explain most
plans:

- Names are exact, case-sensitive
strings. Each resource ID is built
from them ([Names Are Exact String
s](#names-are-exact-strings-names-
are-exact-strings)).
- The state holds only the
arguments that you set. Snowflake
keeps the defaults, and the
provider shows them in read-only
outputs ([State Holds Only What
You Set](#state-holds-only-what-yo
u-set-state-holds-only-what-you-se
t)).

one object, on all objects that
exist now, on future objects, or
by inheritance. The four kinds
look alike in code, but they act
differently ([Four Kinds of Grant]
(#four-kinds-of-grant-four-kinds-o
f-grant)).
- Resources come in stability
tiers, and Snowflake supports only
the newest stable version
([Versions and Stability](#version
s-and-stability-versions-and-stabi
lity)).

integration lets Snowflake assume
an IAM role, and the role must
trust Snowflake back ([Two-Step
Trust with AWS](#two-step-trust-wi
th-aws-two-step-trust-with-aws)).
Last, the resource

that you give it. It manages
objects that have no resource of
their own, and it detects no drift
([Raw SQL Pitfalls](#raw-sql-pitfa
lls-raw-sql-pitfalls)).

Now compare dbt. A common split
gives Terraform the containers and
the access: databases, schemas,
warehouses, roles, grants and
integrations. dbt then builds
tables and views inside them at
each run. The provider's design

Terraform created ([grants design]

one-session-one-role.wrapped_text:
One Session, One Role
A `provider "snowflake"` block holds the
session settings: organization, account, user,
authenticator, role and warehouse. The `role`
and `warehouse` arguments are the defaults of
the session ([provider configuration](https://
github.com/snowflakedb/terraform-provider-snow
flake/blob/v2.23.0/docs/index.md#L167-L177)).
Every statement that Terraform runs uses this
role. The role owns each object that it
creates, so later grants and drops also need
it.

Snowflake divides the admin work between
system roles ([access control considerations](
https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/secur
ity-access-control-considerations)):

- USERADMIN creates and manages users and
roles.
- SECURITYADMIN holds the global MANAGE GRANTS
privilege. It can grant or revoke any
privilege in the account.
- SYSADMIN creates warehouses, databases and
database objects. Custom roles should sit
under SYSADMIN.

The same page advises against ACCOUNTADMIN for
automated scripts. It also warns that by
default "not even the ACCOUNTADMIN role can
modify or drop objects" that a custom role
created, unless that role is granted up the
hierarchy.

To act as several roles, a configuration
declares several provider blocks with aliases.
A resource then picks its session with
`provider = snowflake.<alias>`. The provider
docs forbid `USE ROLE` and `USE WAREHOUSE`
inside SQL, because they make the provider's
results inconsistent ([execute warning](https:
//github.com/snowflakedb/terraform-provider-sn
owflake/blob/v2.23.0/docs/resources/execute.md
#L12)).

Objects and Edges
An object resource manages one Snowflake
object, such as `snowflake_database` or
`snowflake_warehouse`. It has a computed
`fully_qualified_name`. An edge resource
manages a relation between objects that it
does not own, so it has no such field
([identifier guide](https://github.com/snowfla
kedb/terraform-provider-snowflake/blob/v2.23.0
/docs/guides/identifiers_rework_design_decisio
ns.md#L62-L65)). The provider has one edge
resource for each kind of grant ([grant resour
ces](https://github.com/snowflakedb/terraform-
provider-snowflake/blob/v2.23.0/docs/guides/gr
ants_redesign_design_decisions.md#L17-L30)):

- `snowflake_grant_privileges_to_account_role`
grants privileges to an account role.
-
`snowflake_grant_privileges_to_database_role`
grants privileges to a database role.
- `snowflake_grant_account_role` and
`snowflake_grant_database_role` grant a role
to a role or a user.
- `snowflake_grant_ownership` moves ownership
of objects to another role.
- `snowflake_grant_privileges_to_share` and
`snowflake_grant_application_role` cover
shares and apps.

An edge depends on objects that may live
outside Terraform. A grant can name a
warehouse that someone made by hand, or a
table that dbt made. The pitfall Grants on
Unmanaged Objects shows what happens when such
an object disappears.

Names Are Exact Strings
Every field that holds an identifier is
case-sensitive ([identifier guide](https://git
hub.com/snowflakedb/terraform-provider-snowfla
ke/blob/v2.23.0/docs/guides/identifiers_rework
_design_decisions.md#L100-L106)). In Snowflake
SQL, an unquoted name turns into upper case.
So `name = "TEST"` and `name = "test"` are two
different objects, and the second one needs
quotes in every query. Quotes alone, however,
cause no diff. The provider ignores the
difference between `AGENT_WH` and `"AGENT_WH"`
([quoting](https://github.com/snowflakedb/terr
aform-provider-snowflake/blob/v2.23.0/docs/gui
des/identifiers_rework_design_decisions.md#L56
-L60)).

The resource ID follows one rule. If one
Snowflake identifier describes the object, the
ID is its fully qualified name. Otherwise the
ID joins all needed parts with pipes ([ID form
at](https://github.com/snowflakedb/terraform-p
rovider-snowflake/blob/v2.23.0/docs/guides/ide
ntifiers_rework_design_decisions.md#L84-L88)).
Import blocks use the same strings:

| Resource | Import ID |
| --- | --- |
| Account object, such as a warehouse |
`'"NAME"'` |
| Schema | `'"DB"."SCHEMA"'` |
| Schema object, such as a typed stage |
`'"DB"."SCHEMA"."OBJ"'` |
| Grant to an account role | seven parts with
pipes, as in the example below |
| `snowflake_execute` | a random UUID
([execute import](https://github.com/snowflake
db/terraform-provider-snowflake/blob/v2.23.0/d
ocs/resources/execute.md#L154-L160)) |

About the Sources shows how this grant was
imported from a real account and planned:

```text
"AGENT_READ_ONLY"|false|false|USAGE|OnAccountO
bject|WAREHOUSE|"AGENT_WH"
```

The seven parts are the role,
`with_grant_option`, `always_apply`, the
privileges, the kind of target, the object
type and the object name. The configuration
said `account_role_name = "AGENT_READ_ONLY"`
without quotes. The state stored
`"\"AGENT_READ_ONLY\""` with quotes, and the
plan still reported "No changes".

To refer to another object, read its
`fully_qualified_name` instead of joining
names by hand ([identifier guide](https://gith
ub.com/snowflakedb/terraform-provider-snowflak
e/blob/v2.23.0/docs/guides/identifiers_rework_
design_decisions.md#L62-L83)).

State Holds Only What You Set
The provider does not store an optional
argument that the configuration leaves out
([config values in state](https://github.com/s
nowflakedb/terraform-provider-snowflake/blob/v
2.23.0/v1-preparations/CHANGES_BEFORE_V1.md#L4
6-L51)). Snowflake then keeps its own default
for it. To show those values, each resource
has three read-only outputs ([raw output](http
s://github.com/snowflakedb/terraform-provider-
snowflake/blob/v2.23.0/v1-preparations/CHANGES
_BEFORE_V1.md#L53-L59)):

- `show_output` holds the result of `SHOW
<objects>`.
- `describe_output` holds the result of
`DESCRIBE <object>`.
- `parameters` holds the result of `SHOW
PARAMETERS IN <object>`.

Some arguments use special values for "not
set" ([empty values](https://github.com/snowfl
akedb/terraform-provider-snowflake/blob/v2.23.
0/v1-preparations/CHANGES_BEFORE_V1.md#L29-L34
)):

- `"default"` for a boolean that the provider
stores as a string.
- `-1` for a number whose valid range includes
0, such as `auto_suspend`.
- `"<Snowflake Terraform Provider string
default>"` for a string that can be empty.

These values appear in plans. A plan that sets
an argument to `"default"` asks Snowflake to
go back to its own default. The [Terraform map
](../terraform.md#outside-changes-get-reverted
-outside-changes-get-reverted) shows a real
warehouse plan with such lines. To keep a
value, write it in the configuration.

four-kinds-of-grant.wrapped_text:
Four Kinds of Grant
`snowflake_grant_privileges_to_account_role`
grants in one of four ways. Three of them work
like this:

| Kind | Code | What it grants | What destroy
does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One object | `on_account_object`, or
`on_schema_object` with `object_name` |
Privileges on one named object | Revokes them
|
| All | `on_schema_object { all { ... } }` |
Privileges on every object of a type that
exists at apply time | Revokes on every
current object |
| Future | `on_schema_object { future { ... }
}` | A rule for objects created later |
Removes the rule and keeps the grants it made
|

The provider treats a future grant as a
trigger ([on_future decision](https://github.c
om/snowflakedb/terraform-provider-snowflake/bl
ob/v2.23.0/docs/guides/grants_redesign_design_
decisions.md#L85-L91)). It does not track
which objects an `all` grant touched
([always_apply decision](https://github.com/sn
owflakedb/terraform-provider-snowflake/blob/v2
.23.0/docs/guides/grants_redesign_design_decis
ions.md#L77-L84)). So configurations pair an
`all` grant with a `future` grant: the first
covers today's objects, and the second covers
tomorrow's.

The fourth kind is the inherited grant, which
the provider supports since 2.19.0 with an
`inherited` block. One inherited grant covers
every current and future object of a type in a
container. The provider's migration guide
calls the `all` plus `future` pair a common
pattern that an inherited grant replaces
([inherited grants](https://github.com/snowfla
kedb/terraform-provider-snowflake/blob/v2.23.0
/MIGRATION_GUIDE.md#L1986-L1990)). Inherited
grants are a preview feature in Snowflake.
They allow no exception for a single object: a
`REVOKE` on one table appears to succeed, and
the role keeps the privilege ([inherited grant
s](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/in
herited-grants-intro)).

By default, a grant resource manages only the
privileges that it granted. Other grants on
the same object stay. The argument
`strict_privilege_management` makes the
resource revoke privileges that it did not
grant ([design decisions](https://github.com/s
nowflakedb/terraform-provider-snowflake/blob/v
2.23.0/docs/guides/grants_redesign_design_deci
sions.md#L67-L75)).

Future grants in a database need the global
MANAGE GRANTS privilege. By default, only
SECURITYADMIN and ACCOUNTADMIN hold it ([GRANT
privilege](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-r
eference/sql/grant-privilege)).

Versions and Stability
The provider's resources come in three tiers:

- Stable resources are supported.
- Preview resources work only when you list
them in `preview_features_enabled`. They can

Two-Step Trust with AWS
Three Snowflake objects act in AWS through an
IAM role: a storage integration for stages and
Snowpipe, an external volume for Iceberg
tables, and a notification integration. The
[Iceberg in Snowflake map](../../snowflake/ice
berg/snowflake-iceberg.md) explains external
volumes and catalog integrations.

Each side needs a value from the other side.
Snowflake must know the role ARN. The role's
trust policy must name Snowflake's IAM user
and an external ID. Snowflake uses one IAM
user for each account ([storage integration gu
ide](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/
data-load-s3-config-storage-integration)).
Configurations break this loop in one of three
ways:

1. They apply twice. Someone copies
Snowflake's IAM user ARN and external ID into
the AWS code between the two applies.
2. They fix the role ARN in advance by a
naming rule. The integration is created first,
and the trust policy then reads
`describe_output` of the integration.
3. They choose the external ID themselves with
`STORAGE_AWS_EXTERNAL_ID`. Both sides then
know every value before the first apply.
Snowflake documents this option so that one
external ID can serve several integrations and
volumes.

The [AWS map](../aws/terraform-aws.md)
explains the IAM side of the trust.

snowflake-where-to-look-first.wrapped_text:
Where to Look First
Read a Snowflake configuration in this order:

1. `required_providers`. The source tells you
the namespace, and the version tells you how
far the code is from supported behavior. A
committed `.terraform.lock.hcl` tells you the
exact build.
2. Each `provider "snowflake"` block. Note the
authenticator, the role, the warehouse, the
aliases, `preview_features_enabled` and
`experimental_features_*`.
3. The resource types in use. Mark the
deprecated and preview types, and count the
`snowflake_execute` blocks.
4. Each `snowflake_execute`. Check that
`revert` undoes `execute`. Look for `IF NOT
EXISTS`, `OR REPLACE` and secrets in the SQL.
5. The grants. For each one, find its kind,
its level (database or schema) and the role
that owns its target.
6. The `lifecycle` blocks. Look for
`prevent_destroy`, `ignore_changes` and
`replace_triggered_by`.
7. The integrations and their IAM roles. Find
the source of each external ID and IAM user
ARN.
8. The identifier strings. Check the case and
any names joined by hand.
9. The `import`, `moved` and `removed` blocks.
They show what Terraform adopted and what it
renamed.
10. The backend and workspaces. Find which
state, and so which databases, each run
touches.

When a database and one of its schemas both
have future grants for the same object type,

lack the expected privileges. Check with `SHOW

Catalog-Linked Databases Sync Late
A catalog-linked database mirrors the
namespaces of a remote Iceberg catalog. The
provider has no resource for it yet, so
configurations create it with
`snowflake_execute` ([issue 4201](https://gith
ub.com/snowflakedb/terraform-provider-snowflak
e/issues/4201)). Snowflake syncs the tables in
the background, every 30 seconds by default
([CREATE DATABASE (catalog-linked)](https://do
cs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/sql/create-d

tables, so configurations add a wait. Its

sends table drops on to the remote catalog.

One Role per Duty
A single Terraform role with MANAGE GRANTS can
do everything, so every root module and every
environment shares its blast radius.
Snowflake's advice splits the work: USERADMIN
for users and roles, SECURITYADMIN for grants,
and SYSADMIN for objects ([access control cons
iderations](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user

provider alias for each role. The cost is more
provider blocks and more `provider =`
arguments.

the same apply. Nobody copies values, and a

([AWS external ID](https://docs.aws.amazon.com

s_third-party.html)), so it can sit in
configuration.
